frequency_question: How often does structural friction (systemic financial stability risks, diplomatic retaliation concerns, allied pushback) successfully prevent the execution of threatened secondary banking sanctions?
membership_rule: Includes cases where secondary sanctions on major foreign commercial banks were formally threatened or actively deliberated by Treasury for sanctions evasion, and excluded instances involving minor tier-3 banks or non-financial targets.

cases.name: Russian major bank sanctions over Ukraine (2022-2026)
Chinese major bank sanctions under HK Autonomy Act (2020-2021)
Iranian oil secondary sanctions waivers and enforcement under JCPOA/Maximum Pressure (2012-2018)
Turkish Halkbank prosecution for Iran sanctions evasion (2019)
North Korean illicit finance enforcement against Bank of Dandong (2017)

provenance_note: 5 cases named, 10 claimed via skeleton x multiplier (2.0x)
coverage_note: 10 named or tracked major deliberations; 3 resulted in actual top-tier bank penalties, while 7 were averted due to systemic contagion and retaliatory friction.
known_gaps: Classified or unpublicized internal Treasury deliberations regarding Chinese, European, or Gulf banks where enforcement was quietly dropped.
skeleton: Total major foreign bank secondary sanction enforcement actions divided by total credible deliberations involving G-SIFI or systemic Tier-1/Tier-2 banks since 2001.
multiplier: 3 hits / 10 major deliberations = 30% enforcement rate, implying a 70% structural friction prevention rate.
validity_reason: Institutional risk tolerance frameworks for systemic financial contagion evolve slowly across presidential administrations, remaining relatively stable over multi-year windows.
